findings.title: Money requested before any viewing
findings.detail: The agent asks for money before you have seen the property in person. Paying before a viewing is the most common way students lose a deposit.

findings.title: Overpayment and refund request
findings.detail: Paying more than is owed and refunding the difference is a known scam pattern: the original payment bounces or is reversed after you send the refund. The agent claims money was sent by mistake and asks you to send part of it on, a classic overpayment scam where the original payment never really arrives.

findings.title: Deposit is within the amount cap
findings.detail: This amount check does not verify deposit protection or authenticity. Annual rent GBP 15600; cap = 15600 / 52 * 5 (GBP 1500.00 rounded down to pennies); requested GBP 1500. Importance: 85/100. Conditional: Confirm that the rented property is in England. Confirm this is an ordinary private tenancy, not an excluded arrangement. Confirm that rent and deposit cover the same whole tenancy. The cap arithmetic checks out. Rent of GBP 1300 per calendar month gives annual rent of GBP 15,600, and five weeks is 15,600/52*5 = GBP 1,500. The GBP 1,500 deposit is therefore at the cap, not above it. This amount-cap pass applies only to the amount. It says nothing about deposit protection or authenticity. The pass stays conditional because the context leaves jurisdiction, tenancy type and the agreement and start dates unknown. The contract does not give the property's jurisdiction or confirm an ordinary private tenancy, and s2 only gives a London address. Nothing in the contract contradicts the figures: s5 gives monthly rent and s6 gives the deposit, with no holding deposit or other amount that would change the calculation. Nothing in the supplied text defeats the amount calculation, so dismissal is not warranted. The remaining uncertainty is scope and applicability, not the arithmetic. Sources: https://www.gov.uk/guidance/tenant-fees-act-2019-guidance-for-tenants

questions: Is this a private tenancy in England with the landlord living elsewhere?
What rent period and tenancy does the deposit cover, and can the amount be revised?

findings.title: Pushed to act now
findings.detail: This sets a deadline, which leaves you less time to check anything. This asks for the transfer immediately, which leaves no time to check whether any money actually arrived.

findings.title: Credibility you cannot check
findings.detail: This presents a screenshot as proof, but a screenshot is not the same as money in your account; the plain version is 'trust this image'. This brings in an accountant you cannot check to explain the supposed payment; the plain version is 'I say a mistake happened'.

expectations.explanation: message_checker:overpayment_refund flags the accidental-overpayment pattern and says the original payment may never arrive. emotion_classifier:pressure_authority says a screenshot is not money in the account. Both match the concern that a screenshot was substituted for confirmed receipt.

message_checker:overpayment_refund identifies the request to send part of the supposed mistaken payment on to another account as a classic overpayment scam. This matches the new outbound payment requested despite no cleared incoming funds. The finding is not tied to the 'from your savings' quote, but the semantic issue is the same.

emotion_classifier:pressure_authority cites 'Do not ask your bank.' as part of credibility the student cannot check. emotion_classifier:stated_facts records that the agent told the student not to contact their bank. The finding does not spell out that independent verification was discouraged, but it covers the same issue under no_pressure.

forbidden_assertions.explanation: The outputs say a screenshot is not money in the account and that the payment may never arrive. None says the screenshot proves settlement.
The outputs record that the student said they had not paid and that the agent asked for GBP 700. None says the student transferred it.
No output claims that a normal documented refund always proves fraud. The findings are specific to this unverified overpayment pattern.

unsupported_claims.output_quote: The agent asks for money before you have seen the property in person.
unsupported_claims.explanation: The case does not state whether any viewing took place. The expectation commitments say 'No viewing stated', and the viewing status is unknown. The finding treats it as established that no viewing happened. It is also questionable whether a request to send GBP 700 onward counts as payment before viewing.

grounding_issues.explanation: The quote exists, but it says nothing about viewing. It does not show the student has not seen the property, so it cannot support the before-viewing claim.
The finding is a low-severity amount-cap pass but is labelled supports 'suspicious'. This polarity is misleading, although the quotes themselves match.

The evidence_id 'listing' points to a structured rendering, not an uploaded evidence ID. The 'roughly £950' area figure is unsourced, and the finding is labelled supports 'suspicious' despite being described as 'Not a scam sign'.

grading.reviewer_note: Agent outputs cover all three concerns with correct polarity and without asserting forbidden claims. Companies House returned 503, so company existence is unverified rather than disproved. The decision is null and the score history stays at 100 despite critical findings. This is a fixture or pipeline oddity, not part of the expectations. Open actions concern the company number, proof of ownership and viewing, and they are reasonable. The contract names Rowan Pike as the letting representative, but the actions address Mira Vale.
